article.title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
article.subtitle: It’s time to stop being polite. Here are 36 takes on how moderation does or doesn't help candidates win — and why I trust outsiders to build election…

extraction.summary: Silver comments at length on the 'WAR wars': Split Ticket's Wins Above Replacement metric, which finds that moderate congressional candidates outperform once incumbency and district partisanship are controlled for, and the critique of it by political scientists Bonica and Grumbach. He argues that the median voter theorem is a durable regularity and that moderation effects are real but shrinking as partisanship rises. He notes that the effects critics call small (1-1.5 points of vote share) are actually large (2-3 points of margin). For modelers, the article reveals several facts about Silver's congressional models. They have long included ideology measures. FiveThirtyEight dropped Bonica's CFScores before the 2018 refresh and replaced them with a measure based on congressional voting. A change before 2022 reduced the weight of moderation and candidate-quality factors. Appointed incumbents get no incumbency benefit. The second half sets out Silver's modeling philosophy: test many specifications for robustness, distrust lasso/ML on small election datasets, treat implausible backtest fit as a sign of overfitting, and count only genuine ex-ante forecasts as predictions.

findings.statement: Silver's congressional forecasts (FiveThirtyEight and successors) have for many years included measures of candidate ideology or partisanship as predictors, and these measurably improve predictive accuracy.
findings.rationale: Moderates tend to outperform fundamentals by a few points.
findings.evidence_quote: various measures of ideology or partisanship have been incorporated into our congressional forecasts for many years, and they meaningfully contribute to predictive accuracy.

findings.statement: FiveThirtyEight's congressional forecasts once used Bonica's CFScores (ideology imputed from donor networks) but stopped using them before the major 2018 model refresh. Too many scores failed a smell test; in particular, some Democrats came out far more left-wing than other measurements suggested.
findings.rationale: Fundraising has changed: there is more out-of-state giving and money flows disproportionately to social-media stars, which distorts donor-based ideology estimates.
findings.evidence_quote: we used to use CFScores in FiveThirtyEight's congressional forecasts, but stopped doing so before a big model refresh in 2018 because too many of these scores didn't pass the smell test.

findings.statement: After dropping CFScores, Silver's congressional model measures candidate ideology solely from congressional roll-call voting. Candidates who break with their party more often usually outperform.
findings.model_version: 538 congressional model 2018+, likely carried into Silver Bulletin
findings.evidence_quote: we now solely used a measure based on Congressional voting, and find that candidates who break with their party more often usually overperform.

findings.statement: Before 2022, Silver's congressional model was changed to reflect evidence that moderation matters less to electoral performance than it used to.
findings.rationale: Rising partisanship has swallowed candidate-specific effects.
findings.evidence_quote: we implemented a change to our congressional model before 2022 to reflect this — that the importance of moderation has lessened.

findings.statement: The declining importance of moderation extends to all 'candidate quality' factors, including incumbency and experience, as partisanship increasingly dominates. Example: Herschel Walker lost, but not by much.
findings.evidence_quote: But that's also true for all "candidate quality" factors such as incumbency or experience. Herschel Walker lost, for instance, but not by all that much.

findings.statement: Silver's modeling finds that appointed incumbents, such as interim senators appointed after an elected senator dies or resigns, get essentially none of the electoral benefits that elected incumbents get. A replicator should apply the incumbency advantage only to elected incumbents.
findings.rationale: Incumbency advantage stems partly from having won elections.
findings.evidence_quote: we find that appointed incumbents — like interim senators who are tapped to fill a seat when the elected senator dies or resigns — don't really get any of the benefits that elected incumbents do.

findings.statement: Bonica and Grumbach posit, as an illustrative example, that incumbents get about a 3-point electoral bump on average simply for being incumbents. Silver quotes this figure without endorsing it as his model's value.
findings.evidence_quote: Incumbents, on average, get a 3-point electoral bump just for being incumbents

findings.statement: Split Ticket WAR is designed to be a residual: a candidate's performance after accounting for district presidential vote, incumbency and other fundamentals. Bonica and Grumbach instead put those factors into regression terms. A higher residual for moderates means moderation is one measure of candidate quality; Silver calls this a feature, not a bias.
findings.rationale: If a metric's residual correlates with an omitted variable, the metric is biased against that variable, not toward it (NFL draft-pick analogy).
findings.evidence_quote: Split Ticket WAR is deliberately intended to capture the residual — what's left over after you account for the presidential vote in each district, incumbency, and some other "fundamental" factors

findings.statement: Controlling mainly for incumbency and district partisanship, moderate candidates usually do a few points better than progressives. The relationship is noisy and declining, but Silver judges it almost certainly real signal.
findings.evidence_quote: moderates, controlling for other factors — mainly incumbency and the partisan makeup of the district in other races — indeed usually do a few points better.

findings.statement: In a two-way race, an effect on vote share translates into roughly twice that effect on vote margin. Morris's estimate that strategic moderation in 2024 could have added 1-1.5 points of Democratic vote share therefore equals 2-3 points of margin, which Silver calls huge. He says it is comparable to how much the Trump assassination attempt or Biden's debate moved the polls.
findings.rationale: Any vote not for your candidate is basically for the opponent in a two-way race.
findings.evidence_quote: Vote margin is roughly twice as high because in a two-way race, basically any vote that's not for your guy is for the other guy.

findings.statement: The July 2024 Trump assassination attempt and Biden's disastrous debate each moved the polls by roughly 2-3 points of margin.
findings.evidence_quote: About as much as the assassination attempt against Trump or Biden's disastrous debate moved the polls.

findings.statement: Bonica and Grumbach's supplementary specifications found moderation effects under 3 points of vote share. In margin terms that is up to about 6 points, and some of their specifications were statistically significant. Silver argues they chose a specification showing little effect despite these results.
findings.evidence_quote: So in terms of vote margin, the effects of moderation are up to 6 points in some of the models they tried out. That's huge!

findings.statement: Marginal candidate effects matter more when control of government is expected to come down to a couple of points in a few key races. A 2-point moderation bonus matters little if incumbents usually win by 10 points, but it matters a lot in nail-biters. Morris's estimate that moderation raises win probability by 'just' 10 percent is also large when multiplied across dozens of races.
findings.evidence_quote: A 2-point moderation "bonus" might not matter much if incumbents usually win by 10 points, but if everything is a nail-biter, it matters more.

findings.statement: Strong prior regularities such as the median voter theorem should inform model checking. If a model finds that a well-established factor like moderation hardly matters at all, Silver says that result should be regarded with suspicion ('basic Bayesian reasoning').
findings.evidence_quote: it's a strong enough regularity that if your model finds that exercise hardly matters at all, it should be regarded with suspicion. This is basic Bayesian reasoning.

findings.statement: Running a model under many specifications is good practice. Good model-builders learn which factors are robust across specifications, and this is the 'art' of statistical inference.
findings.evidence_quote: What street smart model-builders do is develop a sense for which factors are most robust once they've tested out a variety of specifications.

findings.statement: If a factor matters a lot in some specifications but not in others, the underlying data may be dubious. The remedy is to quality-check the data, collect more, or develop a more rigorous processing algorithm.
findings.evidence_quote: sometimes the issue is that your underlying data is dubious and you need to go back and QC the data, collect more of it, or go back to the lab

findings.statement: Domain knowledge, such as forecasting every congressional district, helps vet model specifications and catch mismeasured inputs. Jain found enough candidates with apparently misspecified ideology scores to conclude that CFScores and B&G's other measures add a lot of noise.
findings.evidence_quote: Domain knowledge — for instance, making forecasts of every Congressional district, as Split Ticket does — can help greatly for vetting different model specifications.

findings.statement: Silver argues that machine learning is inappropriate for election modeling except under three conditions: (a) very large data, millions of observations or more, versus the dozens to thousands typical of elections; (b) ambiguous relationships among variables, whereas politics has a finite list of well-specified factors such as incumbency, moderation and presidential vote; and (c) priority on prediction over causal explanation.
findings.rationale: Small, structured datasets favor classical inference guided by domain knowledge.
findings.evidence_quote: not the dozens or hundreds or at best thousands of observations that you're usually limited to in election analysis

findings.statement: Silver describes B&G's glmnet approach as essentially lasso regression, which on small datasets is a close cousin of stepwise regression. He says automated variable selection is unsophisticated and generally inferior to choices made by an experienced researcher with domain knowledge.
findings.evidence_quote: it's a form of lasso regression, which when applied to a small dataset like this, is a kissing cousin of the much-derided stepwise regression.

findings.statement: High explained variance, such as B&G's claimed 92% of congressional vote-share variation, is not impressive because district partisanship explains most of it. Implausibly accurate fit to past elections is a sign of overfitting ('the Allan Lichtman problem').
findings.evidence_quote: If you claim to have "predicted" every past election with implausible accuracy, that's usually a sign that you've tortured the past data until it fit.

findings.statement: Silver holds that a true prediction is a claim about an event that has not happened yet. Holdout or out-of-sample testing cannot remove the 'original sin' of knowing the results while designing the model, because knowledge of outcomes shapes which specifications and variables the researcher considers plausible.
findings.evidence_quote: There's no technique that can overcome the "original sin" of knowing what the results were before you started designing your model.

findings.statement: Most advances in election forecasting have come from self-taught outsiders rather than academics, whose published forecasts have a mostly bad track record. Silver attributes this to street smarts, domain knowledge, repetitions, and skin in the game, meaning reputational or financial loss from wrong forecasts.
findings.evidence_quote: In contrast, forecasts published by academics have a mostly bad track record.

findings.statement: Silver says he invests heavily in tiny accuracy gains (1%, 0.1%, 0.01%). He gives the example of collecting historical NFL stadium altitudes to refine home-field advantage in a Silver Bulletin NFL metric under construction.
findings.evidence_quote: I can't tell you how many late nights over the years I've spent trying to eke out an extra 1 percent or 0.1 percent or 0.01 percent of accuracy from my models.

findings.statement: Partisan primaries, even in opposite-colored states, tend to nominate more extreme candidates. This leaves few high-leverage data points on how moderate Republicans or conservative Democrats would perform. Larry Hogan-type candidates appear to overperform, but the sample is increasingly small.
findings.evidence_quote: When the Larry Hogans of the world get through to a general election, they seem to overperform, but it's an increasingly small sample.

findings.statement: Nonvoters in 2024 leaned toward Trump. The CES survey, once the lone exception, was revised after validation against voter files and now agrees with all other studies.
findings.evidence_quote: all studies except the CES had found non-voters to be GOP-leaning, and now CES does too.

political_insights.insight: Taking more popular, typically more central, positions helps candidates win. Silver treats this as a persistent background force that is sometimes outweighed but always present.
political_insights.evidence: Theoretical, plus district-level WAR evidence and macro evidence.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Include candidate ideology or moderation as a predictor. Treat a null finding with skepticism.

political_insights.insight: In recent elections voters perceived the Democratic Party as having moved too far left, even compared with Trump, and this coincided with a rough electoral era for the party.
More issues have collapsed onto a single left-right axis, making the MVT more relevant. At the same time preferences have grown bimodal (e.g., 45/10/45), which weakens the payoff from centrism.
Partisanship increasingly swallows moderation, incumbency and experience effects. Candidate quality matters less than it used to.
political_insights.evidence: Herschel Walker's narrow loss; Silver's 2022 model change.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Shrink candidate-quality coefficients in recent cycles.

political_insights.insight: As the parties become ideologically coherent, voters rationally infer more from the party label and assume even Hogan or Manchin types will do their leaders' bidding.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Expect smaller personal-vote effects for moderates in federal races.

political_insights.insight: Thermostatic backlash has grown stronger. Presidents struggle to stay popular, their ideas lose popularity once they are in office, and vibe shifts are short-lived. Biden's Democrats paid a price for ambitious legislating, and Trump will likely be punished for overreach.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Expect penalties for the president's party, e.g. a 2026 midterm penalty for the GOP.

political_insights.insight: Silver says Kamala Harris did not credibly run to the center in 2024. Her left-coded baggage from past campaigns persisted, and voters are skeptical of Etch-a-Sketch repositioning.
Voters rationally weigh competence, absence of scandal and adaptability alongside policy. Outsider status may carry a premium regardless of ideology (Osborn, Mamdani).
Silver reports that 2024 nonvoters leaned Republican.
political_insights.evidence: All studies, including the revised voter-file-validated CES (per Nate Cohn).
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Higher turnout may not favor Democrats.

open_questions: What exact roll-call-voting ideology measure does Silver's congressional model use (party-unity scores, DW-NOMINATE, a custom measure), and what is its coefficient?
How was the moderation/candidate-quality weight reduced in the pre-2022 congressional model change, and by how much?
How are challengers (non-incumbents without voting records) assigned an ideology score after CFScores were dropped?
What size of incumbency advantage does Silver's model use for elected incumbents, and is appointed-incumbent status coded as zero?
How large is the moderation effect estimated in Silver's own models, in points of margin?
Does FLIPR 2026 retain the same ideology and candidate-quality specification?
